--- title: "[Graph.disjoint_union()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the disjoint union of this graph with another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L33501-L33610){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.disjoint_union(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Disjoint union](/assets/graphs/disjoint-union.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G is a triangle on nodes 1, 2, 3 (accent); H is a single edge between its own nodes 1 and 2 (teal). The disjoint union never merges ids: H's nodes are renumbered 4 and 5, giving five nodes in two separate components." width="100%"} Combines graphs by renumbering the other graph's nodes to avoid conflicts. The resulting graph has all nodes and edges from both, with no overlap. The nodes of the calling graph keep their IDs, while every node of `other=` is shifted up by the largest node ID in the calling graph (so with IDs `1` to `3` in the calling graph, `other=`'s node `1` becomes `4`). Edges from `other=` are remapped to the new IDs. Because no node is ever shared, no edge can link the two parts and the result always has at least as many components as the two inputs combined. This is useful for: - assembling a multi-component graph from independently built pieces - putting several networks side by side so one algorithm call covers all of them - building test graphs with a known number of components Neither input is modified; a new `Graph` is returned. If you want nodes with matching IDs to be treated as the same node, use `union()` instead. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to combine with this one. It must have the same directedness as the calling graph. Its nodes are renumbered as described above, and any of its labels that already exist in the calling graph get a numeric suffix (`"A"` becomes `"A_2"`, or `"A_3"` if `"A_2"` is also taken). If either graph is weighted, the result is weighted. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with both graphs combined disjointly: the node count is the sum of both node counts and the edge count is the sum of both edge counts. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Rather than merging on shared node IDs the way `union()` does, `disjoint_union()` renumbers the incoming graph so its IDs sit strictly above the highest ID in the calling graph. Node and edge attributes carry through unchanged. Labels do too, unless one clashes with a label already in the calling graph: labels must be unique, so the incoming one gets a numeric suffix (`"A"` becomes `"A_2"`). The result is a graph with two provably disjoint components, or more when several calls are chained, which is a handy way to assemble a multi-component graph out of independent pieces. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Unlike `union()`, node IDs are never merged here -- even though both graphs use IDs `1`, `2`, `3`, the second graph's nodes are renumbered so the two triangles stay completely separate, giving six nodes: ::: {#21f1111e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Two separate triangles t1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): t1.add_node() t1.add_edges([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)]) t2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): t2.add_node() t2.add_edges([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)]) combined = t1.disjoint_union(t2) combined.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Both triangles keep all three of their edges, so the union has six edges: ::: {#93a7eff0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} combined.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: When both graphs use the same label, the incoming node is relabelled with a suffix so labels stay unique. Here the second graph's `"A"` becomes `"A_2"` and gets ID `3`: ::: {#2ae2efb0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g1 = ec.Graph().add_node(label="A").add_node(label="B").add_edge("A", "B") g2 = ec.Graph().add_node(label="A").add_node(label="C").add_edge("A", "C") g1.disjoint_union(g2).get_node_df().select(["id", "label"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Chaining several calls together is a quick way to build a graph out of multiple independent components: ::: {#3634380e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} component1 = ec.Graph().add_star_graph(5) component2 = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6) component3 = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(4) multi = component1.disjoint_union(component2).disjoint_union(component3) multi.count_weakly_connected_components() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
